report.summary: Reviewed chunk 2 of daedalus/eval/correctness.py: pytest argv construction, ANSI stripping, node id normalization, status parsing with worst-wins ranking, and ManagedProcess-based pytest spawner.

handoff.purpose: Pytest invocation and output parsing: node id normalization, ANSI stripping, status ranking, and ManagedProcess containment.

symbols.name: _git_read
symbols.note: Runs git rev-parse --verify via subprocess, refusing primary checkout; returns CompletedProcess.

symbols.name: resolve_revision
symbols.note: Resolves a revision to full sha via _git_read; returns None on failure or empty output.

symbols.name: pytest_node_argv
symbols.note: Pure function returning argv tuple: sys.executable, -m pytest, node ids, -v, --tb=no, --color=no, -p no:cacheprovider.

symbols.name: _OUTCOME_TOKENS
symbols.note: Maps pytest outcome strings to STATUS_* constants; XFAIL->STATUS_FAILED, XPASS->STATUS_PASSED.

symbols.name: _ANSI_RE
symbols.note: Regex matching full CSI escape sequences: \x1b\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~].

symbols.name: _PROGRESS_RE
symbols.note: Regex for verbose progress line: node and outcome.

symbols.name: _NO_COLLECTORS_RE
symbols.note: Regex for 'ERROR: found no collectors for' line.

symbols.name: _FILE_ERROR_RE
symbols.note: Regex for short-summary file error lines like 'ERROR tests/x.py'.

symbols.name: _norm_node
symbols.note: Normalizes a node string: replace backslashes with slashes and strip.

symbols.name: _same_node
symbols.note: Case-insensitive suffix match; also matches parametrized ids starting with requested + '['.

symbols.name: _STATUS_RANK
symbols.note: Worst-wins ranking: PASSED=0, SKIPPED=1, FAILED=2, COLLECT_ERROR=3, ERROR=4.

symbols.name: parse_pytest_output
symbols.note: Parses pytest text into per-node statuses; never guesses; not_run when silent; missing outranks all; collect_error for uncollectable or file errors.

symbols.name: PytestRun
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass holding statuses, returncode, duration, output, argv, timed_out, containment, error; to_dict returns sorted statuses and output tail.

symbols.name: _spawn_pytest
symbols.note: Runs pytest via ManagedProcess (job object) or subprocess.run; writes output to temp file outside worktree; sets COLUMNS=200.

claims.text: Full sha for ``rev``, or None if it does not resolve.
claims.why: Returns None when proc.returncode != 0; otherwise returns stripped decoded stdout or None if empty.

claims.text: The command line, as a pure function so it is assertable.
claims.why: Function takes node_ids and returns a tuple built solely from sys.executable and node_ids; no side effects.

claims.text: Deliberately close to ``spine.attempt.pytest_gate_argv``: the same interpreter and the same ``-p no:cacheprovider``
claims.why: The referenced spine.attempt.pytest_gate_argv is outside this chunk; cannot compare.

claims.text: It differs in two measured ways, and both are needed for PER-NODE attribution, which ``-q`` cannot give: ``-v`` prints ``<nodeid> PASSED|FAILED|SKIPPED (reason)`` per test, ... ``--tb=no`` the verdict is what is parsed; the traceback is kept in the raw output tail, not in the parse.
claims.why: The argv includes '-v' and '--tb=no', matching the described flags.

claims.text: ``--color=no`` is NOT cosmetic and was NOT here before 2026-07-30.
claims.why: The returned argv includes '--color=no', and the comment explains the FORCE_COLOR incident. The date is historical, uncheckable from code alone, but the flag presence is kept.

claims.text: pytest normally suppresses colour when its output is not a tty, so a captured pipe was assumed to be clean. It is not: pytest honours ``FORCE_COLOR`` (and ``PY_COLORS``) regardless of whether anyone is watching, and a Claude Code session exports ``FORCE_COLOR=3``.
claims.why: This describes external pytest behaviour and environment; not verifiable from this chunk.

claims.text: The per-node line then arrives as tests/test_lib.py::test_x \x1b[32mPASSED\x1b[0m\x1b[32m   [100%]\x1b[0m and ``_PROGRESS_RE`` matches nothing.
claims.why: Given _ANSI_RE strips escapes, the raw line contains escapes; _PROGRESS_RE expects '\S+::\S+' followed by whitespace, but the escape sequence intervenes, so it would not match. Verified by regex logic.

claims.text: MEASURED consequence: pytest exited 0 having collected and PASSED the node, and :func:`parse_pytest_output` returned ``not_run`` for it -- so every candidate was dropped as "not_run on the base revision", no task could ever be seeded, and six end-to-end tests failed.
claims.why: The historical measurement and end-to-end test results are not in this chunk; the parser logic does return not_run for unparsed lines, but the specific incident cannot be confirmed.

claims.text: The parser strips escapes too (see :data:`_ANSI_RE`). Both are deliberate: this function controls its own invocation and asks for clean output, while the parser is a pure function that may be handed output it did not invoke.
claims.why: pytest_node_argv includes '--color=no'; parse_pytest_output strips ANSI via _ANSI_RE on every line.

claims.text: Every CSI escape sequence, stripped from a line before it is matched.
claims.why: The regex matches CSI sequences: ESC [ parameter bytes (0x30-0x3F) intermediate bytes (0x20-0x2F) final byte (0x40-0x7E), which is the full CSI definition.

claims.text: The assumption this replaces was "pytest does not colour a pipe". It does, when ``FORCE_COLOR`` or ``PY_COLORS`` is set, and the environment this project is developed in sets ``FORCE_COLOR=3``.
claims.why: External pytest behaviour and environment claim; not verifiable from this chunk.

claims.text: The full CSI form rather than just ``\x1b\[[0-9;]*m``: pytest also emits cursor and erase-line sequences, and a parser that handles only colour would be correct until the day the terminal width changed.
claims.why: The regex matches any final byte in @-~, including cursor movement (H, A, B, C, D) and erase (J, K), not just 'm'.

claims.text: "ERROR: not found: C:\...\tests\x.py::test_y" -- the FILE collected, and the node id is not in it. The task named a test that does not exist.
claims.why: The regex matches '^ERROR: not found:' and captures the node; the comment describes the scenario.

claims.text: "ERROR: found no collectors for C:\...\tests\x.py::test_y" -- a DIFFERENT fact, and conflating the two was a real defect in this parser, caught by running it: the file itself could not be collected (it imports something that does not exist on the base revision, which is the NORMAL state of a test added by the fix being evaluated). That is a test that does not pass -- a valid FAIL_TO_PASS before-state -- whereas "not found" refutes the task. Reporting the second as the first invalidated 13 of 14 nodes of a real corpus candidate.
claims.why: The parser treats _NO_COLLECTORS_RE separately from _NOT_FOUND_RE, assigning STATUS_COLLECT_ERROR instead of STATUS_MISSING, and the comment describes the defect. The historical '13 of 14' is uncheckable, but the distinction is implemented.

claims.text: Three spellings have to compare equal, and all three were measured on this box rather than assumed: pytest prints node ids relative to its rootdir on progress lines, and as an ABSOLUTE path in the ``not found`` line -- so this is a normalised SUFFIX match, not equality; Windows spells the same file two ways, so it is case-insensitive; a PARAMETRIZED test is requested as ``file.py::test_x`` and reported as ``file.py::test_x[1]``, once per case. Those report lines belong to the requested node (see :func:`parse_pytest_output`, which reduces several outcomes for one node to the WORST of them, so one red case cannot be averaged away by two green ones).
claims.why: _same_node does case-insensitive suffix match (r == q or r.endswith('/' + q)) and parametrized match (r.startswith(q + '[') or '/' + q + '[' in r). The worst-wins reduction is implemented in parse_pytest_output via _STATUS_RANK.

claims.text: Worst-wins ranking when one requested node produces several report lines (parametrized cases). A single red case makes the node red -- averaging is exactly the move that hides a fatal blind spot behind an acceptable number.
claims.why: The rank values order PASSED < SKIPPED < FAILED < COLLECT_ERROR < ERROR, and parse_pytest_output only replaces status when observed rank is greater than current rank.

claims.text: Per-node status for every requested node id. Never guesses. A node the output says nothing about is ``not_run`` -- not a pass, not a fail. An explicit ``not found`` (``missing``) is final and outranks everything, because the node does not exist; otherwise several report lines for one node reduce to the WORST outcome seen (see ``_STATUS_RANK``); a node with no line of its own inherits ``collect_error`` if its FILE failed to collect.
claims.why: Initializes all requested to STATUS_NOT_RUN; missing set applied last and unconditionally overwrites; statuses only updated when rank greater; file_errors cause STATUS_COLLECT_ERROR for silent nodes whose file matches; uncollectable also set to STATUS_COLLECT_ERROR.

claims.text: ANSI escapes are stripped before ANY match is attempted. A coloured PASSED is still a pass, and reading it as `not_run` is the worst available failure: it is indistinguishable from a test that never ran, so it silently removes evidence instead of reporting that the evidence could not be read.
claims.why: Line is stripped via _ANSI_RE.sub('', raw).strip() before any regex match.

claims.text: One pytest invocation, with its raw output kept rather than summarised.
claims.why: PytestRun stores full output string; to_dict only includes output_tail, but the object itself keeps the full output.

claims.text: Run pytest and return ``(returncode, output, timed_out, containment)``.
claims.why: Function returns exactly that tuple, as seen in the code (though the final return is cut off, the structure is clear).

claims.text: Preferred path is :class:`daedalus.spine.cancel.ManagedProcess`, i.e. a Windows Job Object with KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, so a hung or forking test tree dies with the run -- the same containment the repo's own pytest gate uses. If that backend is unavailable the run still happens through ``subprocess.run`` and SAYS SO in ``containment``, because a quietly weaker containment that nobody can see is worse than a named one.
claims.why: The function attempts ManagedProcess; on CancellationUnavailable falls back to subprocess.run; containment is set to 'job_object' when ManagedProcess succeeds, otherwise remains 'none' (initialized). The claim about the repo's own gate is uncheckable, but the behaviour is as described.

claims.text: Output goes to a file OUTSIDE the worktree: a pipe deadlocks on a chatty run while the parent is polling instead of reading (measured in ``spine.attempt.pytest_gate``, whose shape this follows).
claims.why: Creates tempfile.mkdtemp and opens out_path inside it; passes the file handle as stdout to both ManagedProcess and subprocess.run.

observations.what: _FILE_ERROR_RE matches any line starting with 'ERROR ' followed by a non-space path, but the filter requires the path to contain '/' and no '::'. A path like 'tests/x.py' matches, but a Windows path 'C:\tests\x.py' normalized contains slashes? Actually normalization replaces backslashes with slashes, so it would match. However, a node id like 'tests/x.py::test_y' also starts with 'ERROR '? No, the regex requires '^ERROR\s+(?P<path>\S+?)' and node ids contain '::' which is excluded by the '::' not in path check. But a file error line could be 'ERROR tests/x.py - KeyboardInterrupt' which matches. The filter also requires '/' in the normalized path, which excludes bare filenames like 'test_x.py'. That seems intentional but could miss errors where pytest prints only a filename without a path.

In parse_pytest_output, the file_errors matching uses 'qfile.endswith('/' + fe)' which could cause false positives if a requested file path ends with the error path as a suffix. For example, requested 'tests/foo/x.py' and error 'foo/x.py' would match. This is intended for suffix matching, but the asymmetry (both directions) could be overly broad.

The _PROGRESS_RE pattern uses '\b' after the outcome, but the progress line includes '   [ 50%]' after the outcome. The '\b' will match at the boundary between the outcome and the following spaces, so it works. However, if the outcome is followed by a non-word character like ':' (e.g., in some pytest versions), it might not match. The comment shows the format with spaces, so it's pinned to that.

The _spawn_pytest function sets COLUMNS=200 but does not set PYTHONUNBUFFERED or similar; however, output is redirected to a file, so buffering is not an issue. The code is cut off before the final return statement, but the structure is clear.

When ManagedProcess is unavailable and subprocess.run times out, it raises TimeoutExpired, which is not caught in this chunk; the function would propagate an exception rather than returning timed_out=True. The docstring says it returns timed_out, but the subprocess.run path does not handle timeout. However, the code is cut off before the except block; the chunk ends at the subprocess.run call. The try/except structure might catch it later, but from this chunk it appears unhandled.
